title: Fuel Cost Split Calculator: Share a Trip Fairly
description: Split a trip's fuel cost evenly across passengers with the Fuel Cost Split Calculator — total in, fair shares out. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a $109.29 fuel bill split four ways is $27.32 each — a number nobody at the fuel stop has to negotiate.
quick_answer: The Fuel Cost Split Calculator divides a journey's total fuel cost among the people sharing the ride and returns each person's share. Enter the trip's fuel total — from the Fuel Cost Calculator or a handful of receipts — and the passenger count, and read the split to the cent.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
An even split: total fuel cost ÷ number of people, to the cent, with the rounding visible rather than hidden.
Do I need an account?
No. Total and headcount in, shares out.
Can I rely on this for professional work?
For informal cost-sharing and club travel, yes. Formal expense policies have their own rules; this is the arithmetic friend groups and carpools actually use.
Does the route include live traffic?
No — the split divides a total that already happened or is estimated; traffic is inside the total, not the division.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
It is why the fuel total is what it is. The split itself only needs the total.
Should the driver pay a share?
Custom varies: many groups exempt the driver for providing the car and the driving. The calculator gives the even split; your group's custom adjusts it.
What if passengers ride only part-way?
Weight the split by legs ridden — split each leg among its riders and add each person's legs. Fairness scales; arithmetic keeps up.
Someone joined for one leg only.
Split per leg: each leg's fuel divided among its riders, summed per person. The principle — divide what each shared — scales to any manifest.
We also split tolls — same tool?
Add tolls to the total before splitting if the group agrees they are shared costs; divide fuel-only if that was the deal. The deal comes first, the division second.
Rounding left a cent over.
It always might. Convention gives it to the driver — see the table note on this page.
